title: Building and costing the wine list
lead: Running the list as a business: what a great list does, pricing bottles and glasses, buying through the three tiers and allocations, and keeping the cellar counted and moving.

intro.title: THE LIST IS THE PROGRAM
intro.text: Four formulas run a wine program month to month. All money examples in this chapter are our own round numbers.

sections.name: What a great list does
sections.source: Court of Master Sommeliers, 2025 Advanced and Master standards and Advanced Practical guide; Wine Spectator Restaurant Awards criteria; Cornell School of Hotel Administration

lines.label: The standard
lines.text: The Court's 2025 standards start service with a beverage list that is clean, accurate, up to date and easy to read.

lines.label: What judges want
lines.text: Wine Spectator's award judges want complete, accurate entries (vintages, appellations, full producer names) and a list that matches the menu in price and style.

know: Wine Spectator's Award of Excellence starts at 75 selections; Best of Award of Excellence lists typically run 350+; Grand Award lists typically 1,000+.
Grand Award lists show depth in mature vintages and large formats, and every Grand Award winner is inspected.
A Cornell study of 270 restaurants linked four list traits to higher wine sales: the list on the food menu, prices without a dollar sign, well-regarded wineries and a reserve or special section.
The same study linked organizing the list by style (sweet, bold, dry) to lower sales.
The Advanced practical includes correcting a beverage list full of mistakes, big and small.

sections.name: Pricing the list
sections.source: Court of Master Sommeliers, Curriculum Guide (Business of the Sommelier); Restaurant Business; Provi; SevenFifty Daily

lines.label: From Level 2
lines.text: Cost % = bottle cost ÷ list price, and list price = cost ÷ target cost %. At Master level you set one policy across the whole list.

lines.label: The scale
lines.text: Trade guides put bottle markups at about 2 to 4 times cost, and most operators use a sliding scale: cheaper bottles marked up more, expensive ones less.

know: The simplest by-the-glass rule prices one glass at the wholesale cost of the whole bottle.
If a bottle sells only 3 or 4 glasses before it's past its best, price per pour on the glasses you really sell.
Gross profit is price minus cost: a pricier bottle at a higher cost % can still earn more dollars.
An allocated wine can be priced up to match its rarity, or left as a value find.
When a guest questions list prices, acknowledge it and explain the house pricing policy tactfully.

sections.name: Buying: tiers, distributors and allocations
sections.source: TTB (importing); eCFR 27 CFR part 6; VinePair (three-tier explainer); SevenFifty Daily (allocations)

lines.label: Three tiers
lines.text: In the US, wine generally moves from producer or importer, to wholesaler (distributor), to retailer, and a restaurant is a retailer. Each state has its own laws on how that works.

lines.label: Importers
lines.text: An importer needs a federal Basic Importer's Permit and an approved label (COLA) for each product, and must meet state and local rules too.

know: Federal rules call producers, importers and wholesalers 'industry members'; anyone selling to consumers, restaurants included, is a 'retailer'.
An importer that wholesales wines it didn't import also needs a Wholesaler's Basic Permit.
Federally, supplier credit beyond 30 days from delivery is a means to induce, and state law still applies on top.
Allocated wines are those where demand outstrips supply; producers often split them by market and favor long-standing buyers.
Distributors and importers may ask for a by-the-glass placement or a long-term commitment for an allocation, and skipping an allocation can cost you the next one.

items.name: Producer or importer
items.text: Makes the wine or brings it into the US

items.name: Wholesaler
items.text: Stores, ships and sells to retailers

items.name: Retailer
items.text: Shops, bars and restaurants sell to guests

items.name: Buy steadily
items.text: Support suppliers through the year, not only when the rare bottle lands.

items.name: Be honest
items.text: Tell reps your direction and how much you can really buy.

items.name: Ask the market
items.text: Your distributor's team knows what reaches your area.

items.name: Know when to pass
items.text: No allocation is worth buying wines you won't be proud to pour.

sections.name: The cellar: storage, inventory and turnover
sections.source: Court of Master Sommeliers, Hospitality & Service Standards (2023) and 2025 Advanced and Master standards; BevSpot; MarketMan

lines.label: From Level 2
lines.text: Store at a constant 50–60°F, corked table wines on their side, spirits and fortified wines upright, organized and away from light, odors and vibration.

lines.label: Counting
lines.text: Usage = starting inventory + what came in − ending inventory. Every other number starts from an accurate count.

know: Serve the oldest stock first (FIFO); the Court writes it into beer service.
Par level = (weekly usage + safety stock) ÷ deliveries per week.
One trade guide puts safety stock at about 20–30% of weekly usage.
Inventory turnover = COGS ÷ average inventory, where average inventory = (beginning + ending) ÷ 2.
The Court expects sommeliers to run, clean and maintain Coravin systems: gas canisters, needles and all.

3× markup and 33% cost describe the same price: one multiplies cost, the other divides it.

facts.fact: Mise en place: beverage lists are clean, accurate, up-to-date and easy to read; beverages are stored in an organized manner and stored and served at the correct temperature.

The Advanced Business of the Sommelier exam covers beverage alcohol program management: qualitative assessment for pricing, theme and style; marketing and sales techniques; purchasing; costing; audits; list management; inventory management; staff management and training; beverage equipment management. Exercises include costing, reading and evaluating inventory sheets, and correcting a beverage list with lots of mistakes, big and small.
The example MS Practical & Tasting feedback report lists Business of the Sommelier as a Practical portion alongside the Sparkling and Decanting tables.

Wine Spectator: a wine list must present complete, accurate information, including vintages and appellations; complete producer names and correct spellings are mandatory; overall presentation is considered.

Award of Excellence: at least 75 selections, a well-chosen assortment of quality producers and a thematic match to the menu in price and style. Best of Award of Excellence: typically 350 or more selections, excellent breadth across multiple regions and/or significant vertical depth of top producers, superior presentation. Grand Award: typically 1,000 or more selections, outstanding depth in mature vintages, large-format bottles, excellent harmony with the menu, superior presentation; all Grand Award winners and many others are inspected.

Cornell (Lynn and Yang): tested 46 attributes of wine lists in 270 restaurants; four linked with higher sales: list on the food menu, prices without a dollar sign, wines from wineries known for quality, a reserve or special section. Organizing by wine style (sweet, bold, dry) was connected with lower sales. A longer list reaped more sales only at casual restaurants, up to about 150 wines. Price had no relationship with sales at fine dining. The research is correlation, not causation.
Cost % = bottle cost ÷ list price; list price = bottle cost ÷ target cost %.
Gross profit is revenue minus cost of goods sold.
Wine pricing multipliers can range from 2× cost to 4× cost; most operators supplement this with a sliding scale, with cheaper bottles marked up higher than expensive ones.

The most basic by-the-glass strategy prices a glass at the wholesale cost of the bottle; a per-pour approach divides the bottle price by the glasses; if only three or four pours are sold from a bottle instead of the full six, adjust the per-glass price.

Allocated (highly allocated) bottles are those for which demand outstrips supply. Some are allocated to regions based on percentage of business, and often go to the best, longest-standing customers. Relationships and steady buying through the year help. Distributors and importers often require a by-the-glass placement or long-term buying commitment for certain allocations. If you don't take an allocation you can lose it. Laws on allocations vary among states. An allocated wine can be marked up to match its rarity or kept as a hidden gem. No allocation is worth buying wines you won't be proud to offer.
Pricing complaints: acknowledge the guest's opinion and tactfully state the restaurant's pricing policies.

The three-tier system: the manufacturer sells to a wholesaler, who sells to the retailer, who sells to the public. Tier 1 is producers and importers; tier 2 distributors/wholesalers handle storage, transportation and marketing; tier 3 retailers include bottle shops, restaurants and bars. Each state has its own laws on alcohol distribution under the 21st Amendment.
27 CFR 6.11: 'industry member' means a producer, importer or wholesaler of distilled spirits, wine or malt beverages; 'retailer' means any person selling them to consumers.
27 CFR 6.1: nothing in part 6 exempts any person from the requirements of any State law or regulation.

Importers need a Federal Basic Importer's Permit (TTB F 5100.24) and must keep a US business office; to sell at wholesale beverages other than those they import, they also need a Wholesaler's Basic Permit; they must hold a TTB Certificate of Label Approval (COLA) for each unique product/label at the time of importation; they must also meet State and local requirements.
27 CFR 6.65: extension of credit by an industry member to a retailer for more than 30 days from the date of delivery is a means to induce.
27 CFR 6.72: requiring a retailer to purchase one product in order to obtain another ('tie-in' sales) is a means to induce.

Storage (Court Hospitality & Service Standards): constant temperature, 50-60°F / 10-15°C ideal for long-term storage; organized; cork-finished table wines on their side; spirits and fortified wines upright; avoid light, vibration, heat and temperature swings; away from odors.
Beer service: always follow FIFO (first in, first out), serving the oldest stock first.
Coravin: sommeliers should know pouring, recharging (sparkling), cleaning, replacing gas canisters and changing the needle for the Timeless, Pivot and Sparkling systems.
Continuously over- or under-ordering creates problems for bars and increases costs and customer dissatisfaction.

Usage = starting inventory + inventory added − ending inventory. Track sitting inventory in one unit of measurement, used continuously. Par level = (weekly usage + safety stock) ÷ number of deliveries in a week; safety stock should generally be around 20-30% of weekly usage.
Inventory turnover ratio = cost of goods sold ÷ average inventory; average inventory = (beginning + ending inventory) ÷ 2; a low ratio shows too much inventory or low sales.

unverified: Markup ranges vary by source: Restaurant Business gives 2× to 4× cost; a Provi article gives '200-300 percent over retail'; vendor pages give other ranges. Only the Restaurant Business range is stated, as one guide's figure; the sliding-scale table is our own example.
Wine Spectator's 350+ and 1,000+ counts are 'typical', not minimums; only the 75-selection figure is stated as a floor.
Cornell's findings are correlations from one 2009 study, not proof of cause.
The 20-30% safety stock figure is one vendor's (BevSpot) general guide, not an industry standard.

Whether a particular allocation deal ('buy X to get Y', a required by-the-glass placement) breaks federal tie-in rules depends on the facts and on state law; the lesson says to check, not that such deals are unlawful.
VinePair's figures for markups at each tier (about 50% at tier 1, 150% or more overall) were not confirmed elsewhere and are not used.
State rules on credit, samples and allocations differ by state and are not described; no state's rule is presented as ours.

read.bigIdea: Accurate, built for the food, and easy to buy from.
read.where: The Court treats the list as **mise en place**: clean, accurate, up to date, easy to read. At Advanced it hands you a **beverage list full of mistakes** to correct. Award judges look for the same accuracy, plus fit with the **menu**.

stops.name: Accuracy
stops.text: Every entry carries **vintage**, **appellation** and the **full producer name**, spelled right. Wine Spectator calls complete names and correct spelling **mandatory**.

stops.name: Range and depth
stops.text: **Breadth** means many regions. **Depth** means verticals of top producers and **mature vintages**. Wine Spectator's top two levels typically run **350+** and **1,000+** selections.

stops.name: Fit
stops.text: The list matches the menu in **price** and **style**. In Cornell's study, a longer list lifted sales only at **casual** restaurants, up to about **150** wines.

stops.name: Layout
stops.text: Cornell linked four traits to higher sales: list on the **food menu**, **no dollar signs**, well-known wineries, a **reserve** section. Sorting by **style** went with lower sales. It's correlation, not proof.

read.mixup: **Breadth** is how many regions and styles the list covers. **Depth** is how far it goes into one producer or region: verticals and mature vintages.
read.sayIt: The list follows the menu; I'm happy to point you to a few that fit your dishes.

read.bigIdea: Price for the dollars, not just the percent.
read.where: From Level 2: **cost %** = cost ÷ price. A program lead sets one **pricing policy** for the whole list, then checks it against what sells.

stops.name: Bottles
stops.text: One trade guide gives **2× to 4× cost**. Most operators use a **sliding scale**: the cheapest bottles carry the biggest markup.

stops.name: Why a scale
stops.text: Example: a $10 bottle at 4× is $40 (25% cost, $30 profit). A $100 bottle at 2× is $200 (50% cost, **$100 profit**). Higher cost %, more dollars.

stops.name: By the glass
stops.text: Simplest rule: one glass costs the guest what the **whole bottle** cost you. If only **3 or 4 glasses** sell before the bottle fades, price on those.

stops.name: Rare bottles
stops.text: An **allocated** wine can be priced up to its rarity or left as a value find.

read.mixup: **Markup** multiplies cost: a $10 bottle at 3× is $30. **Cost %** divides it: $10 ÷ $30 = 33%. Same price, two ways to say it.
read.sayIt: This one is one of the best values on the list right now.

read.bigIdea: Every bottle comes through three tiers.
read.where: In the US the **three-tier system** separates **producers and importers**, **wholesalers** and **retailers**. A restaurant is a retailer. Federal rules apply everywhere, and each **state** has its own laws on top.
read.stopsTitle: Four stops on the way in

stops.name: Importers
stops.text: Foreign wine comes in under a **Basic Importer's Permit**, with a **COLA** for every label. An importer selling other companies' wines at wholesale needs a **Wholesaler's** permit too.

stops.name: Distributors
stops.text: The wholesaler stores, ships and sells to you, and your rep knows what reaches your **market**. Federally, supplier credit can't run past **30 days** from delivery.

stops.name: Allocations
stops.text: When **demand outstrips supply**, wines are split by market and tend to go to steady, **long-standing** buyers. Skip your allocation and you may lose it.

stops.name: Strings attached
stops.text: Some suppliers want a **by-the-glass placement** or a long-term commitment. Federal rules list a **tie-in** (buy one product to get another) as a means to induce, so check deals against your state's rules.

read.mixup: An **importer** brings wine into the US under a federal importer's permit. A **wholesaler** sells to retailers; an importer selling other people's wines needs that permit too.

keyPoints.line: constant, for long-term storage.
oldest stock goes out first.
start + received − end, for the same period.
(weekly usage + safety stock) ÷ deliveries a week.

read.bigIdea: Count it, store it, keep it moving.
read.where: A cellar is money on a shelf. Store it right, count it on a schedule and set a **par** for every wine you pour, so you neither run out nor over-order.

stops.name: Storage
stops.text: From Level 2: a constant **50–60°F**, corked wines on their **side**, spirits and fortified wines **upright**. Rotate **FIFO**: oldest stock out first.

stops.name: Count
stops.text: **Usage** = start + received − end. Pick one unit of measure and count the same way every time.

stops.name: Par
stops.text: **Par** = (weekly usage + safety stock) ÷ deliveries a week. Example: 12 bottles a week plus 3 safety, one delivery: par is **15**.

stops.name: Turnover
stops.text: **Turnover** = COGS ÷ average inventory. Example: $120,000 ÷ $30,000 = **4** turns a year. Low turnover means too much stock or slow sales.

read.mixup: **Par** is how much you keep on hand. **Turnover** is how often your stock sells through. Too much stock shows up as low turnover.
